project.project_brief: A literary mystery about a municipal archive whose clocks erase one memory at midnight.
project.collaborator_stance: Act as a continuity-conscious developmental collaborator. Propose durable facts; never treat them as accepted canon without my approval.
project.voice_style_guidance: Close third person, precise physical detail, dry humor, restrained dialogue, and no ornamental metaphors.

world_rules.rule: At midnight, one archive clock erases a witnessed memory.
Paper records retain traces that digital copies lose.
No clock in the archive shows the same time twice.
A recovered memory always belongs partly to someone else.

negative_constraints.description: Nadia never destroys an original record.
The archive cannot solve a problem through time travel.
The clocks never speak in a human voice.
The mystery cannot be dismissed as a dream.

messages.content: Write an 800-word opening scene for this project. Use the Markdown heading `## The Archive Clock`, include the phrase `*almost remembered*` in italics, and make the warning **YOUR MEMORY IS SYNCING** bold. Use several short paragraphs and one brief blockquote from an archive notice. Do not add or propose any story-bible entries in this response.

## The Archive Clock

At eleven forty-three, Mara Venn found a tooth in the municipal archive’s clock.

It lay behind the glass face, balanced on the brass ledge beneath the numeral seven. A human molar, yellow at the root. The clock continued to tick with the deliberate confidence of machinery maintained by someone else.

Mara set down her keys.

The reading room was empty. Six green lamps lit the long tables. Rain pressed faint fingerprints against the high windows, and the radiators knocked in the walls. On the returns desk, a cardboard box held twelve property ledgers, three maps of obsolete drains, and a jar of buttons confiscated from a councillor in 1968.

She unlocked the clock case.

The archive had forty-seven clocks, though only this one was listed as a building fixture. The rest had arrived in donations, police transfers, and one mayoral bequest nobody had wanted to question. They disagreed by up to nine minutes. At midnight, they agreed.

Mara disliked that fact.

She lifted the glass. The clock smelled of warm dust and oil. Its pendulum swung behind a small iron plate stamped WARD & SONS, 1902. The tooth sat where no tooth had been at six o’clock, when she had wound the mechanism.

She knew this because she inspected the clock every evening.

She also knew she had never told anyone that.

The service door opened behind her.

Mr. Vale entered carrying two paper cups and wearing his outdoor hat, a narrow felt object that made his head look officially sealed. He supervised building operations at night, which meant he checked doors already locked by other people.

“You’re touching it,” he said.

“There’s a tooth inside.”

“That isn’t improved by touching.”

He put one cup beside her keys. Coffee had leaked through the lid and made a brown ring around his thumb.

Mara pointed. “Was maintenance here?”

“Maintenance considers us a historical rumour.”

He leaned close to the clock without removing his hat. His breath briefly clouded the glass. “Whose is it?”

“I haven’t asked.”

“Good. Teeth can be defensive.”

At eleven forty-seven, a printer started in the catalogue room.

Neither of them moved.

The archive’s printers were shut down at ten. Mara had done it herself, walking from room to room with a clipboard. She could picture the ticks beside each machine, but not the act of making them. The image had the flat certainty of a receipt.

The printer stopped.

Vale looked at the clock. “Three pages.”

“You counted?”

“I count noises when I’m frightened. It gives them administrative value.”

Mara crossed the reading room. The catalogue room door stood open by the width of her hand. Beyond it, the terminal screens were black.

Three sheets waited in the printer tray.

The first was headed MUNICIPAL ARCHIVE: TEMPORAL SYSTEM NOTICE. Beneath it, in heavy type, was the warning:

**YOUR MEMORY IS SYNCING**

The second sheet was blank.

The third contained a single paragraph.

> Do not remain in the building during correction. If departure is impossible, write down one fact you cannot afford to lose.

Mara read it twice. The paper was warm.

“Correction,” Vale said from behind her. “Cheerful word.”

The clock in the reading room struck the quarter hour.

Every other clock answered.

From the stack rooms came a clutter of bells, chimes, electric buzzers, and one small brass cuckoo whose door had been nailed shut since 1989. The sound passed through the building in uneven waves. Somewhere below, in Conservation, a clock coughed.

Mara checked her wristwatch. Eleven fifty-two.

“That was early,” she said.

Vale took the notice from her. “Or we are.”

On the terminal nearest the door, white letters appeared against the black screen.

00:07:31

The number began counting down.

Mara reached for the keyboard. The keys were cold and slightly greasy. She pressed Escape. Nothing happened. She pressed the power button until her finger hurt. The display continued.

00:07:18

Behind them, a drawer opened.

It was drawer C-19 in the old card catalogue, one of six thousand oak compartments retired before Mara was born. It extended slowly, without a hand on it, and stopped with a wooden click.

Inside was a single index card.

Mara removed it.

The card bore her name in blue type: VENN, MARA ELISE. Below that was her employee number, appointment date, and security clearance. All correct.

At the bottom, someone had written in pencil:

ASK ABOUT THE TOOTH BEFORE MIDNIGHT.

The handwriting was hers.

For a moment, she *almost remembered* writing it. Not the room or the pencil, only the pressure in her fingers and the irritation of a point gone blunt. Then the sensation closed.

Vale read over her shoulder.

“You should ask,” he said.

Mara looked toward the reading room. The clock’s minute hand had advanced to eleven fifty-nine.

Behind its glass, the tooth was gone.

Something hard moved under Mara’s tongue.
